OBNUARY REFERENCE 
MR CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Gundappa Korwar, a former Member of this House on 4th 
May, 2003, at the age of 64 years. 
Born at village Korwar in Gulbarga District in December, 1939, Shri 
Korwar had his education at Shri Sharanabasaveshwar School and 
Government college, Gulbarga. An agriculturist by vocation, Shri Korwar left 
the studies and joined the movement for enlightening the Scheduled Castes 
and organised students against the sufferings of Dalits including movement 
for temple entry of Dalits in Shri Sharanabasaveshwar, Rajya Gudi and Ram 
Mandir in Gulbarga. He took special interest in the uplift of downtrodden, 
children and women. He also arranged mass marriages of disabled and worked 
for the removal of untouchability. He participated in various agitations which 
aimed at providing land to the landless tillers. He was associated with various 
social and welfare organisations in different capacities. 
Shri Korwar represented the State of Karnataka in this House from 
April, 1992 to April, 1998. 
In the passing away of Shri Korwar, the country has lost a noted 
parliamentarian and a distinguished social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Gundappa Korwar. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark 
of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the Members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Health Schemes in Rajasthan 
*601. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the on-going family welfare and rural health schemes in Rajasthan with 
Central assistance; 
(b) whether any scheme is being run with foreign assistance; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) The following Family Welfare and Rural Health Schemes/projects 
are under implementation in Rajasthan with the Central assistance:— 
1. Sub Centre Scheme. 
2. Urban Family Welfare Centres. 
3. Urban Health Posts. 
4. Sterilisation Bed Scheme. 
5. National Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS). 
6. IEC activities under RCH. 
7. Assistance to NGOs. 
8. Compensation to acceptors of Sterilisation and IUD. 
9. Assistance under EAG Scheme. 
10. Provision of Transport. 
(b) and (c) The following Family Welfare and Rural Health Schemes/ 
projects are under implementation in Rajasthan with external assistance:— 
1. Minor Civil Works: A sum of Rs. 10 lakh has been provided per district for all 
districts for arrangements of water and electricity and repair works at PHC. Rs. 
290 lakhs have been provided for the purpose from World Bank Assistance. 
2. Major Civil Works: A sum of Rs. 10.00 lakh has been provided for each 
CHC/District hospital for construction and upgradation of OT/Labour Room 
and arrangement of water and electricity, Rs. 889.47 lakh have been 
provided from World Bank Assistance. 
2 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
3. Contractual appointment of Additional ANMs in 30% Sub Centres in 'C 
category districts. Against the total requirement of 1193 additional ANMs the 
State Government has so far engaged 690. 
4. Contractual Appointment of Public Health Nurse (PHN)/Staff Nurse (SN) in 
25% PHCs/CHCs in 'C category districts and 50% PHCs/ CHCs in B category 
Districts. 54 PHN have been so engaged against a target of 267. 
5. Contractual Appointment of two Lab Technicians in each district. 17 
Lab Technicians have been engaged against the requirement of 64. 
6. Hiring of Anaesthetists for emergency obstetric care in sub-district hospitals, 
CHCs and FRUs @ Rs. 1000/- per case. Rs. 5.65 lakh has already been 
released to the State. 
7. Hiring of Safe Motherhood (SM) Consultant for Medical Termination of Pregnancy 
(MTP) in PHCs/CHCs to visit once a week or at least once a fortnight on a fixed 
day for performing MTPs and providing ante- natal check-ups etc. @ Rs. 
800/- per day visit. 
8. Hiring of other Contractual Staff: There is provision of hiring of Contractual 
Staff including Sahayikas at sub- centre. 529 Sahayikas have been hired. 
9. 24 Hour Delivery Services at PHCs/CHCs in all the 32 districts. There is 
provision of Rs. 200/- for doctor, Rs. 100/- for ANM and Rs. 30/- for cleaner 
for each night delivery performed. 
10. Referral Transport of Pregnant women to First Referral Units (FRUs) 
For providing referral transport to pregnant women of poor families for 
emergency obstetric care Rs. 72.05 lakhs have been provided to 18 
districts. 
11. Training of Dais: Dai Training under RCH Programme is directed towards 
improving delivery services in rural areas. Six districts of Rajasthan viz. 
Alwar, Banner, Chum, Hanumangarh, Jaisalmer and Jalore are covered 
under the Scheme. A sum of Rs. 22.03 lakh has been released to these 
districts. 
12 Holding RCH Camps: In order to provide the RCH services to people living in 
remote areas where the existing services at PHC level are underutilized, a 
scheme for holding camps has been initiated. All districts of Rajasthan are covered 
under the Scheme. 989 such camps have already been organised in Rajasthan. 
3 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
13. Outreach Services: Outreach services under RCH Programme is directed towards 
awareness generation and improvement in quality of care and strengthen 
immunization. The activity is being initiated in 5 districts of Rajasthan viz, 
Sawai Madhopur, Banner, Bharatpur, Udaipur and Banswara. A sum of Rs. 
26.40 lakh has been released to these districts in 2000-01 and Rs.36.96 lakh 
in 2001-02. 
14. Pulse Polio Programme: Pulse Polio Programme for eradication of Polio 
from Rajasthan is under implementation. During 2003 National Immunization 
day was observed through out the State on 5th January, and 9th February, 2003. 
During January around 1,12,55,298 children and during February 1,14,69,343 
children were given polio drops. Moreover, in the high risk districts of the State, 
Sub-National Immunization Day was observed on 6th April, 2003. Three more 
SNIDs will be held in the State in 1st June, 2003, September, 2003 and 
November, 2003. 
15. RCH Sub Project in Jaipur City and Tonk: RCH sub-project is being 
implemented in two districts viz. Jaipur City and Tonk. A sum of Rs. 
1115.00 lakh has been released by GOI for these 2 sub projects (Rs. 473.00 
lakh for Jaipur City and Rs. 64.00 lakh for Tonk) for different activities like 
Civil Works, IEC Innovative Activities, Procurement, Baseline Survey, 
Hiring of staff etc. 
16. UNFPA assisted Integrated Population and Development Project: 
UNFPA assisted Integrated Population and Development Project is under 
implementation in 6 districts of Rajasthan namely Alwar, Bhilwara 
Udaipur, Chittorgarh Bharatpur and Swai Madhopur, at a total cost of Rs.42.82 
crores w.e.f. 21st Dec, 1998 ending on June, 2003 with the aim of achieving 
population stabilization through provision of Reproductive Health 
Services. 
17. European Commission (EC) assisted Sector Investment Programme is 
under implementation in Banner and Jalore districts of Rajasthan. 
Rs. 11.15 Cr. have since been released and Rs.43.52 Cr. is further estimated 
since 1-4-02. The Programme has been extended to another 8 districts, 
namely Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Nagaur, Pali, Sirohi, Bikaner, Dungarpur and 
Banswara.

SHRI KB. KRISHNAMURTHY : Sir, without admitting the resource 
crunch, the hon. Minister has mentioned that only four out of the 52 low-power 
transmitters were upgraded in Karnataka. The (a) part of my question is: I would 
like to know, at this rate, how far the Prasar Bharati will be made professional in 
generating surplus funds for modernisation and upgradation of DD centres? 
The (b) part is, why is the Government burdening itself with allocation of more 
transmission time for themes of social welfare, health care, adult education, 
literacy, family planning, etc., leaving little scope for airing commercial 
programmes to bring in more revenue through advertisements, like private 
channels? Part (c) of my question is, why should not the Government impose on 
all private TV channels, a minimum stipulated transmission time for the coverage 
of social welfare programmes and for rural coverage? 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, as far as the first part of his question 
is concerned, the Prasar Bharti has conveyed to us that they are already engaged 
in the whole process of expansion and development of the existing Doordarshan 
facility in the country. As a part of the Tenth Five Year Plan, a big amount of 
Rs. 319 crore has been earmarked only for the development of the programme 
content and an amount of Rs. 100 crore has been earmarked for upgradation of 
studio facility, new equipment, etc. Out of these, in Karnataka alone, 
approximately an amount of Rs. 25 crore is going to be expended on improvement 
of the content programme facility and about Rs. 10-11 crore are going to be 
spent on upgradation of studio equipment. As far as your two interlinked 'b' 
and 'c' parts of the question are conc erned, as a public broadcaster, 
Doordarshan Prasar Bharti Radio have a commitment and the commitment is 
that they shall not join the naked race for commerce and revenue only; they 
shall emphasise upon the public character which is enjoyed by the Prasar Bharti 
Act. Yes, your point is very well taken that we need to improve the social 
content further. We are doing health programme, education programme, etc. We 
have held the Gyan Darshan programme. All these are going on. In addition to 
that, even at the local level, the regional channels are supplementing. Therefore, 
this is an ongoing process. Yes, as a Minister in the Government of India, we are 
only urging upon them the need to become more professional and competitive.

Health care cost 
*604. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a.) whether the escalating health care cost is causing indebtedness among rural 
poor; 
(b) if so, the magnitude of increase in the health care cost during the last 
decade, and 
(c) how Government propose to ensure that the poorer segments of the 
population are able to access health services required by them at reasonable 
cost? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Different studfes and surveys indicate that escalating health care costs is one of 
the reasons for indebtedness, especially among the rural poor. 
14 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
(b) Data on unit cost of treatment per episode in hospitals/outpatient 
clinices, particularly in the private sector is not available. Hence, the cost 
comparisons are based on expenditure (out-of-pocket spending category) 
indicated by households surveyed by NSSO. The average total expenditure for 
inpatient-outpatient treatment/episode during the period 1986-87 and 1995-96 is 
as under:

 Rural     Urban Rural   Urban 
For outpatient treatment/episode 76          79 176       194

(c) The main objective of the Government's health policy is to achieve an 
acceptable standared of good health amongst the general population of the 
country by adopting the approach of increasing access to the decentralized 
public health system, by establishing new infrastructure in deficient areas and 
by upgrading the infrastructure in the existing institutions. Overriding importance 
would be given to ensuring a more equitable access to health services across 
the social and geographical expanse of the country. Health being a State subject, 
State Governments are primarily, responsible for providing health facilities to 
the people. Each State Government seeks to achieve better health care for its 
people through a variety of measures including, the implementation of several 
National health programmes, establishment of a comprehensive network of rural 
health infrastructure, renovation and modernization of health infrastruture and 
augmentation of medical manpower, particularly in rural areas. 
Free health care services are provided to the poor. Medicines are generally 
provided free of cost to the in-patients in the Government hospitals and under 
various health programmes, which are under implementation for control of 
majontiseases^ike Malaria, TB, Blindness, Leprosy and AIDS. In order to ensure 
availability of drugs at reasonable prices, the Government has been promulgating 
the Drugs (Price Contral) Order under the Essential Commoditinos Act, 1955, 
from time to time. 
Under Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana, Additional Central Assistance 
is provided to States /UTs, to further the goal of primary health care, through 
strengthening and improving the functional status of the primary health care 
institutions. 
15 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
To enable easy access of our less advantaged citizens to good health services, 
and to offer health protection, of some choice, the public sector general insurance 
companies have also been encouraged to design a community based universal health 
insurance scheme. 
The National Health Policy, 2002, envisages increasing public health 
investment to 2% of GDP by the year 2010 from the existing level of 0.9%. Therein, 
it is also proposed that State Governments would increase their expenditure on health 
sector to 7% of their total budget by 2005 and to 8% of the budget by 2010. The Central 
Government contribution would rise from the existing level of 15% to 25% of the total public 
health spending by 2010. The Government is making all out efforts to increase 
expenditure on health as per policy, subject to the overall financial constraints.

Statement 
(a) Exports have indeed recovered sharply in 2002-03. While the growth in 2001 -02 
was negative at 1.7%, in 2002-03 merchandise exports have increased by 18.05% to reach 
the provisional figure of US $ 51.7 Billion. The innovative initiatives in Exim Policy of 
2003-04 aim at sustaining the growth in order to reach the medium term objective of 
merchandise exports of US $ 80 billion by 2006-07. 
(b) The war in Iraq has not impacted exports significantly. Apart from temporary 
disruption in supplies under Oil for Food Programme, higher cost had to be incurred by 
exporters on account of ocean freight, insurance and disruption in transportation. 
(c) and (d) In the flew Exim Policy, the Government has launched a new Scheme 
to facilitate and to promote export of Services by allowing duty free import of 
consumables, office and professional equipment, spares and furniture upto 10% of the 
foreign exchange earnings on actual user basis. In the case of recognised hotels of the 
category of 3-Star and above and other registered service providers in this sector, the 
entitlement is limited to 5% subject to some restrictions. The scheme will cover service 
providers who have an average foreign exchange earnings in excess of Rs. 10 lakhs in 
the preceding three licensing years. The scheme is expected to provide impetus for 
Services exports in which India has a competitive advantage due to availability of 
qualified manpower.

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
Statement 
Health being a state subject, it is for various State Governments to ensure 
provision of adequate facilities for treatment of cancer. The Government of India is 
augmenting the State Governments' efforts in provision of early detection, diagnosis 
and treatment facilities for cancer under various components of National Cancer Control 
Programme (NCCP) which was initiated in 1975 and revised in 1984-85. The emphasis of 
this programme is to address the problem of inadequate and unevenly distributed cancer 
therapy facilities in the country and thereby ensure easy access to cancer treatment 
facilities either free or at nominal cost to the needy all over the country. Details of 
various schemes implemented under the National Cancer Control Programme are annexed 
as Statement-I {See below). 
Besides (Govemment run hospitals and Medical College hospitals, 20 Regional 
Cancer Centres have been set up under NCCP where treatment to poor patients is 
available either free or at nominal cost. Poor patients living below poverty line can also 
avail of financial assistance from National Illness Assistance Fund (NIAF) now known as 
Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN) being operated by the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare. 
At present there is no proposal to introduce Cancer Insurance Scheme through 
Regional Cancer Centres. 
Statement-I 
National Cancer Control Programme 
Development of Oncology Wing in Medical College Hospital 
This scheme is available only for Government Medical Colleges to fill up the 
geographical gaps in the detection and treatment of cancer in the country. Financial assistance 
up to Rs. 2.00 crores is provided to an Institute under the scheme for purchase of 
equipments like Cobalt Machine, Brachytherapy etc. This is a onetime grant 
Setting up of Cobalt Therapy Unit 
Financial assistance up to Rs. 1.50 crore is provided to State Government for setting 
up of Cobalt Therapy Unit in Government Institutions. 
An amount of Rs. 1.00 crore is provided for Cobalt Therapy Unit to the Non-
Govemmental Organisations.

The Mammography equipment has also been included under the scheme for setting 
up of Cobalt Therapy Unit. A Central Assistance up to Rs. 30.00 lakhs is provided to those 
Institutions/Organisations who have the facilities for treatment of cancer patients and has 
well-equipped Radiotherapy Department. All these are one-time grant. 
District Cancer Control Programme 
A scheme of district project (duration-five years) lor health education, detection 
and pain relief measures under National Cancer Control Programme was initiated 
during the year 1990-91. In this scheme, financial assistance of Rs. 15.00 lakhs is 
provided to the State Govemment/UT administration for each district selected under the 
scheme with a provision of Rs. 10.00 lakhs per annum for each district for the remaining 
four years of the project period. After five years, the project is to be taken over by the 
State Government. 
Financial Assistance to Registered Voluntary Organisations 
Under the schemes, assistance upto Rs. 5.00 lakhs is provided to the 
Voluntary organistions for undertaking health edcuction and early detection activities 
in cancer on the specific recommendations of the State Government. 
Regional Cancer Centers 
This Ministry has recognised 20 Regional Cancer Centres in different States/ UTs. 
The Chittaranjan National Cancer Institutes, Kolkata and Institute Rotary Cancer 
Hospital (IRCH), AIIMS, New Delhi have got a different funding pattern. Remaining RCCs 
are paid an amount of 75.00 lakhs annually. These RCCs extend treatment facilities and 
conduct research in the field of Cancer.

 WHO Survey on smoking in films 
*614. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the recent World Health Organisation (WHO) survey 
on about 400 Hindi, Tamil and Telugu films revealed that instances of smoking in films 
have gone up from 22 per cent to 53 per cent in the last ten years i.e from 1991 to2002; 
(b) if so, the details of the survey; and 
(c) the steps Government are taking to reduce smoking habit in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) According to survey commissioned by WHO, 76% of 
the films studied portrayed tobacco consumption. Smoking incidence amongst lead 
actors has risen sharply from 22% in 1991 to 53% in 2002. The survey analyzed the 
portrayal of tobacco in Indian cinema and the impact it has on the youth audiences. It 
reported that there has been a meteoric rise in the incidence of smoking in Indian films 
over the last decade and this has resulted in the youth having a more positive attitude 
towards smoking. The findings of the study called for a multi-sectoral approach to 
reduce smoking portrayal in films and all other electronic media that reaches the youth 
not only in India but the entire South East Asia region. 
Apart from several other legislative and administrative steps taken by the 
Government, a comprehensive bill to discourage consumption of tobacco products 
has been passed by the Parliament on the 30th of April, 2003. The Bill, inter-alia, 
contained provisions prohibiting smoking in public places, a total prohibition on all 
forms of direct and indirect advertising, prohibition on sales to minors and prohibition on 
sale of tobacco products within a radius of 100 yards of educational institutions. It also 
contains provisions for more explicit warnings including pictorial warnings. 
The World Health Organization has announced "Tabacco Free Films and 
Fashion" as the theme for observance of World No Tobacco Day on 31 st May, 2003. 
The Government will also be utilizing this opportunity to highlight the ill effects of 
tobacco and advocate the elimination of portrayal of use of tobacco in films.

is one of the critical factors for achieving higher economic growth; 
(b) whether the Budget proposal for the year 2003-04 envisaged any reliefs/ 
incentives with a view to strengthening the export efforts; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reason therefor ?

INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAPRUDI): (a) Yes, Sir. The Economic Survey 
58 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
2002-03 has emphasized that exports hold the key to achieving a sustainable balance 
between the requirement of higher growth and ensuring viability of external sector. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. Promotion of exports is one of the five priorities envisaged in the 
Union Budget 2003-04. Several measures covering merchandise goods and services 
exports have been taken in the Union Budget 2003-04. These include reduction in 
custom duty on imports of capital goods and other inputs required for export

†4488. SHRI DATTA MEGHE : Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian exports have not yet become competitive in 
international market in terms of cost and quality due to which we have not been able 
to achieve success in the field of exports; 
(b) whether annual export of India is still hanging around 5 billion dollars; 
(c) if so, whether Indian goods are in position to compete in international market 
in terms of cost and quality; and 
(d) if so, the details of efforts being made by Government to suitably amend the 
export policy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) to (c) No, Sir. Indian exports are 
competitive both in terms of cost and quality and the annual export of India is not 5 billion 
dollars, in fact, India's exports of merchandise goods is US $ 51.7 billion in 2002-03. India 
has attained a growth rate of 18.05% exceeding the target of 12% despite the depressing 
World Economic and Trade Environment. As per WTO, India's export growth rate in 
2002 at 15 % is the second highest among the thirty leading exporters of merchandise 
goods in the world. All this reflects the level of India's export competitiveness in the 
global market. 
(d) Export promotion being a constant endeavour a medium term Export Strategy 
to be co-terminus with the Tenth Plan Period (2002-07) was announced in January, 2002 
with the objective of achieving 1 % of world exports. In line with

Authenticity of ISO certifying agencies 
4489. SHRI B.P. SINGHAL : Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
<a) whether there is any system to check if ISO certifying agencies which 
have issued certificates were actually authorised to do so; 
(b) if not, the credibility or authenticity of such certificates; 
(c) whether Government are aware that in the reimbursement proforma there 
is no provision to ensure that an SSI unit is actually complying with ISO norms 
and standards, before the reimbursement is sanctioned; 
(d) if so, why this should not be made mandatory before reimbursement is 
given; and 
(e) the details of subsidies and all schemes which are currently in vogue in 
granting of subsidies for obtaining ISO certification ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI CHENNAMANENIVIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) and (b) At 
present, the activities of Indian/foreign agencies granting ISO 9000 arid ISO 
14001 certificate operating in India are not being monitored by any Government 
agency as the process of certification is voluntary and not mandatory. There is 
no process for official registration of such ISO certifying agency. The certificates 
that are being issued by the certification bodies which are signatory to the 
Multilateral Arrangement (MLA) of mutual recognition are considered credible 
and authentic. The accreditation mark on the certificate is the authority for the 
certifying agency to issue the certificates. The accreditation mark can also be 
verified by any individual or department to verify the authority to issue ISO 
certificates. The validity and scope of the accreditation of the certifying agency 
can be verified from the website of the respective accreditation council. The 
60 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
Quality Council of India which is a registered autonomous Society set up through a joint 
initiative of the Government and industry associations, has also established a National 
Accreditation Board for Certification Bodies (NABCB) which, in turn, is a signatory to the 
MLA and also provides accreditation to certifying bodies. 
(c) and (d) Cases for reimbursement are considered for approval by the 
Screening Committee set up under the Chairmanship of Additional Secretary & 
Development Commissioner (SSI). The Committee is represented by expert members 
from the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Standardization Testing and Quality 
Certification (STQC) body under the Department of Information Technology and 
Quality Council of India (QCI). BIS and STQC are also certification agencies accredited by 
International Accreditation Bodies. 
Office of the Development Commissioner, Small Scale Industries while 
considering requests for reimbursement checks: 
(i)   that ISO 9001/14001 certificate have "Logo" and the Accreditation 
number of the Accreditation body, 
(ii)  that ISO 9001/14001 certificate have complete address of the location/ site 
which has been certified; and 
(iii) the validity of the ISO 9001/14001 certificate i.e. date of issue and date of 
expiry. 
In addition, an internal study is also undertaken by Office of the Development 
Commissioner, Small Scale Industries, with the assistance of its field offices i. e. 
Small Industries Service Institutes (SISIs) to ascertain the compliance with ISO norms 
and standards etc. 
Further the National Productivity Council has been assigned a study on all India 
basis to assess the impact of ISO 9001/14001 reimbursement scheme in terms of 
improvement in productivity, export performance and quality management 
installed by the unit etc. 
(e) Some Departments of the Government of India encourage the industry to follow 
the international standards like ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 by providing a token 
assistance. 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries Office of Development Commissioner (SSI) 
have been implementing a Scheme under which 75% of the expenses incurred by SSI units in 
acquiring Quality Management System - ISO 9001 certification, are reimbursed 
(restricted to Rs. 75,000). The validity of the Scheme has been 
61 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
extended up to 31.3.2007. The scope of this Scheme now has been extended to provide 
reimbursement of expenses of acquiring Environmental-Management System (EMS) 
ISO 14001 Certificate w.e.f. 18.10.2002.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Government is aware of the problem of 
manufacture and sale of spurious drugs. As per the feedback available from the State 
Licensing Authorities during the period 1999-2000,2000-2001 and 2001-
2002,35570,36947 and 38824 samples were tested and out of which 115,112 and 96 
samples were found spurious respectively. Thus, there does not appear to be 
proliferation of spurious drugs in the country. 
83 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) Since manufacture and sale of spurious drugs is mainly a clandestine activity 
indulged in by anti-social persons, steps are taken from time to time by enforcement 
authorities of the States to detect and unearth spurious/fake drugs in the inter-state 
commerce. Government of India has taken the following steps: 
The Drugs Controller General (India) has advised the State Drugs Controllers to take 
the following measures for curbing the incidence of spurious drugs: 
I (i)   Constitution/reactivation of the State Drugs Advisory Committee in 
which various State and industry associations as well consumer 
association would find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate intelligence-cum-legal machinery with police 
assistance. Training should be provided to selected officials of Drugs 
Control Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, 
prosecution etc. in respect of spurious/counterfeit drugs. 
(iii) To ensure speedy analysis of drug samples by establishing own State level 
drug testing facilities. 
(iv) State Drugs Control Authorities should be cautious while approving licences 
for drug products to ensure that "look alike" products are not encouraged. 
(v) To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures. 
(vi) Surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(vii) Engaging experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
(viii) Cooperation of pharmaceutical industry by regular interaction with them. 
(IX) Collection of survey samples under National Survey Quality Evaluation of 
Drugs (NSQED) programme. 
II The Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare had written on Oct. 8, 
2002 to all the Chief Ministers seeking their personal intervention to ensure 
that adequate measures are taken in each State to deal with this problem. 
Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare also convened a meeting of the 
Health Ministers and senior officials of 13 major States of the country on 12- 
11-2002 to discuss measures to ensure concerted action required to check 
movement of spurious drugs in the country and to involve all stakeholders, 
including pharma industry, to curb the menace of manufacture and marketing 
of spurious/fake medicines.

Spread of AIDS among Women 
4546. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a feet that the number of HTV infected women around the 
globe has increased from 41 per cent in 1997 to 49.7 per cent in 2002; and 
118 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
(b) the action Government propose to take to check the spread of AIDS among 
the women ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. As per UNAJDS and WHO 
AIDS "epidemic update" December 1997 and December 2002, the proportion of HIV 
infected women around the globe during year 1997 and 2002 was 39.5 per cent and 
45.7 per cent respectively. 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AJDS in all segments of 
population including women in the country, Govt, of India has launched a 
comprehensive National Aids Control Programme, currently under 
implementation throughout the country as a centrally sponsored scheme with the 
following components:— 
> Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change communication. 
> Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes for 
blood safety, volurtary counselling and testing services. 
> Prevention of parent to child transmission of HTV, information education and 
communication (IEC) & awareness building among adolescents and 
sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine Initiative. 
> Provisions of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
> Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-private partnerships. 
> Building technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and 
Evaluation, Technical resource groups, operational reasearch and 
Programme management.

S ARS symptoms in the Country 
4552. SHRIRAJKUMARDHOOT: 
SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that certain persons have shown Suspected Acute 
Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) symptoms in metros in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) how these persons have been isolated and treated; and 
(d) the preventive steps taken against SARS? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) No case of Severe Acute 
Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) has been reported in India which conform to the 
WHO case definition. However, as on 1st May, 2003, twenty laboratory positive 
(PCR) test) persons have been reported. They are from the States of 
Maharashtra (15) West Bengal (2), Tamil Nadu (1) and Punjab (1 initial PCR test 
positive). 
(c) As a matter of abundant precaution the cases were isolated and treated 
in identified hospitals. 
123 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) Keeping in view the implications of an epidemic, Government of India has 
taken necessary steps which include the following: 
• A High level Centre-State Joint Committee has been formed for close 
monitoring of the situation and providing technical assistance to all State 
Governments. Related technical inputs including patient management 
protocol, standard operating protocol and transfer protocol have been provided 
to the State Governments. 
• Mandatory Screening has been introduced in all Ports and Airports for all the 
persons disembarking in India and a proforma has been prescribed for such 
purpose. The health care facilities at such Airports and Ports have been 
strengthened by deploying additional doctors and evolving a standard 
operating protocol. Health counters for screening have been opened in all such 
Airports and ports. The health staff is monitoring passengers of flights 
and ships arriving in India. 
• Facilities for treatment of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome in isolation have also 
been arranged in the Central Government Hospitals as also in other infectious 
Diseases Hospitals. The State Governments have identified hospitals with 
isolation facilities for treatment of SARS. 
• To meet the immediate requirements, Central Goverment is procuring special 
respirators from Defence Research Development Organi ation for 
distribution to State Governments. 
• Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has obtained the required primers 
for preparing reagents to diagnose the viruses believed to be causing SARS. 
National Institute of Communicable Diseases, Delhi and National Institute of 
Virology, Pune have been identified as the nodal agencies for laboratory 
investigation of any suspect/probable case.

Increase in diabetes in the country 
4565. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA:  
SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state; 
(a) whether India has been declared the diabetes capital of the world; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that more and more juvenile are falling prey to this 
disease, 
(d) whether it is also a fact that unless concrete steps are taken to combat this 
disease, the diabetic population in India will rise to 5.72 crore by 2025; and 
(e) the measures taken by Government to arrest the increasing trend of this 
disease among the children and to accelerate steps to spread awareness among 
masses? 
THE MINISTER OF STAIE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) There is no nation wide data collection regarding 
the number of people suffering from diabetes. However, it has been estimated that in 
1995, 19.4 million individuals were affected by diabetes in India & these numbers are 
expected to increase to 57.2 million by the year 2025. Indian Council of Medical 
Research have estimated that about 10% of the diabetics in the country are in the 
juvenile age group. 
(e) Since Diabetes is a Lifestyle related disease, it is very important to adopt 
preventive lifestyle intervention for control of diabetes among the children and the 
adults in the country. These interventions are being emphasized through 
Information, Education and Communication (IEC) activities of the Government including 
through Central Health Education Bureau (CHEB).

4576. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY :  
        DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY : 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the bleeding Indian film industry needs to release its business model 
to recover the losses it has made in terms of revenue generation in the calendar year 
2002; 
(b) if so, whether experts have pointed out that Indian film industry should 
look at the "studio model" of the 1930s to turn its fortune; 
(c) whether the industry has urged Government to help it to grow during the 
calendar year 2003; 
(d) if so, whether any concession have been provided in the budget of 2003-04; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) and (b) The film 
industry in India is in the private sector. The Government does not maintain statistics 
relating to the revenue earned by the industry. However according to a report on the 
industry brought out by FICCI and KPMG titled "The Indian Entertainment Sector—
In the Spot Light", the Indian film industry is estimated to have lost nearly Rs. 3 
billion on gross revenues of Rs. 39 billion during the year 2002. 
As per projections made in the report the industry is likely to break-even within 
the next 18-24 months, the upswing being driven by consolidation, increasing 
corporatisation and an eventual integration of various components of the industry viz. 
production, distribution and exhibition. Over the next five years, films produced by 
large organised houses are projected to grow to around 55% from the current 
level of 20%. 
(c) to (e) In order to facilitate a greater flow of institutional finance to the film 
industry, a notification dated 16.10.2000 was issued by the Ministry of Finance, 
whereunder 'Entertainment industry including films' has been specified as an 
approved activity for extending loans under the IDBI Act. The 
151

Reserve Bank of India has also evolved guidelines to enable commercial banks to 
fund film production. These steps have eased the flow of institutional finance into film 
production. In addition, the FDI regime for films has been further liberalised. Several 
tax concessions have also been given to the film industry during successive budgets. 
In the budget 2003-04, audio CDs have been exempted from the levy of Central 
Excise Duty.

Statement 
Guidelines for applying licenses for setting up Community Radio Stations 
PREAMBLE 
The Union Government has decided to grant Community Broadcasting licenses 
to well established educational institutions/organizations recognized by the Central 
Government or the State Government. These will include the Universities and 
Institutes of Technology/Management and residential school. 
The salient features of eligibility criteria, basic conditions/obligations and 
procedures for obtaining license to set up and operate Community Radio Service are 
briefly described below :— For further details reference may be made to Ministry 
of Information and Broadcasting. 
2. Technical Parameters: 
2.1 Licence will be granted for FM transmitters for power of 50 Watts or less. 
2.2 Licence will be issued in the shared frequency band from 87.5 to 100 Mhz. 
However, in the event of frequency not being available in this band, the exclusive 
broadcast band of 104 to 108 Mhz. may also be considered, as in case of private FM 
broadcasters. The frequency band from 100 to 104 Mhz. earmarked exclusively for the 
use of AIR, Prasar Bharati will not be disturbed. 
3. Procedure to be followed : 
Application : 
3.1 Any eligible institution/organization desirous of setting up of 
Community Radio Broadcasting Service may make an application to the Ministry 
of I & B in the prescribed proforma. (Download application form). 
3.2 The Ministry of I & B immediately on receipt of an application will consult 
the Wireless Advisor in WPC Wing of Ministry of Communications and also Prasar 
Bharati to determine the availability of frequency at the place requested by the 
applicant. 
3.3 The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting will refer the eligible 
applicant case to the Ministries of Home Affairs, Defence, Human Resource 
Development and External Affairs and letter of intent and/or license will be issued 
only after getting the requisite clearances from these Ministries. The licensee will be 
required to sign a licence agreement after allotment of frequency by WPC. The license 
agreement shall specify detailed terms and conditions under which the licence is to 
be operated. 
153 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
3.4 Within one year from the date of signing of licence agreement, the applicant 
will complete all necessary formalities such as obtaining SACFA clearance etc., set up 
the necessary broadcast facilities and obtain a Wireless Operating Licence from the 
Wireless Advisor in the WPC Wing of the Ministry of Communications and 
Information Technology. 
3.5 In the event of more than one claimant for a single frequency at a given 
place, the licensee will be selected by a Committee constituted by the Ministry of I & 
B on the basis of standing commitment, objectives and resources of the applicant 
organization. 
3.6 Licensee will be charged only the spectrum usage fee as determined by the 
WPC. The Ministry of I & B will not levy any other licence fee. 
4. Terms and Conditions: 
4.1 The basic objective of the Community Radio Broadcasting would be to serve 
the cause of the community in the service area of the licensee by involving members 
of the community in the broadcast of their programmes. For this purpose community 
would mean people living in the coverage zone of the broadcasting service of the 
licensee. 
4.2 The licence shall be for a period of three (3) years. 
4.3 The licence shall not be transferable. 
4.4 An applicant will not be permitted more than one licence. 
4.5 The licensee shall provide its services on free to air basis. 
4.6 The licensee shall not use its channel/broadcast services in whole or part for 
commercial purposes. 
4.7 The programmes on the community radio service will focus on issues relating 
to education, health, environment, agriculture, rural and community development. 
The content must be confined to social, cultural and "local issues and the format, 
subject, presentation and language must reflect and exude the local flavour and 
fragrance. 
4.8 The licensee shall not be permitted to broadcast any news and current affairs 
programmes and shall not air election and political broadcasts. 
4.9 The licensee shall not air any advertisement or sponsored programmes. 
4.10 The licensee shall ensure that nothing is included in the programme 
of the licensee which : 
(a)  Offends against good taste or decency; 
154 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
(b) Contains criticism of friendly countries; 
(c) Contains attack on religions or communities or visuals or words 
contemptuous of religious groups or which promote communal 
attitudes; 
(d) Contains anything obscene, defamatory, deliberate, false and 
suggestive innuendos and half truths; 
(e) Is likely to encourage or incite violence or contains anything against 
maintenance of law and order or which promote anti-national attitudes; 
(f) Contains anything amounting to contempt of court; 
(g) Contains aspersions against the integrity of the President and 
Judiciary; 
(h)  Contains anything affecting the integrity of the Nation; 
(i) Criticises, maligns or slanders any individual in person or certain groups, 
segments of social, public and moral life of the country; 
(j)   Encourages superstition or blind belief; 
(k)  Denigrates women; 
(I)   Denigrates children; 
(m) May present/depict/suggest as desirable the misuse of drugs including 
alcohol, narcotics and tobacco or which may stereotype, incite, vilify or 
perpetuate hatred against or attempt to demean any person or group on the 
basis of ethnicity, nationality, race, gender, sexual preference, religion, age 
or physical or mental disability. 
4.11 The licensee shall ensure that due care is taken with respect to religious 
programmes with a view to avoiding :- 
(a) improper exploitation of religious susceptibilities; and 
(b) offence to the religious views and beliefs of those belonging to a 
particular religion or religious denomination. 
 
4.12 That the licensee shall ensure that due emphasis is given in the 
programmes to promote values of national integration, religious harmony, scientific 
temper and Indian culture. 
4.13 The licensee shall follow the Programme Code of All India Radio. 
4.14 The licensee shall pay spectrum usage fee as determined by the Wireless 
Advisor in WPC Wing. 
155 

[5 May, 2003J RAJYA SABHA 
4.15 Though the licensees will operate the service under the Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting, Government of India, the licensing will be subject to the 
condition that as and when any regulatory authority to regulate and monitor the 
broadcast services in the country is constituted, the licensees will have to adhere to the 
norms, rules and regulations prescribed by such authority. 
4.16 The licensee shall provide such information to the Government on such 
intervals as may be required in this connection, the licensee is required to preserve tapes 
of programmes broadcast during the last six months failing which the Government will 
be at liberty to revoke the licence. 
4.17 The Government or its authorized representative shall have the right to 
inspect the'broadcast facilities of the licensees and collect such information as 
considered necessary in public and community interests. 
4.18 The Government reserves the right to take over the entire services and 
networks of the licensee or revoke/terminate/suspend the licence in the interest of 
national security or in the event of national emergency/war or low intensity conflict 
or similar type of situations. 
4.19 All foreign personnel likely to be deployed by way of appointment, contract, 
consultancy, etc. by the licensee for installation, maintenance and operation of the 
licensee's services shall be required to obtain security clearance from the Government 
of India. 
4.20 The Government reserves the right to modify at any time the terms and 
conditions if it is necessary to do so in the interest of the general public or for the 
proper conduct of broadcasting or for security considerations. 
4.21 Government may revoke the licence at any time in public interest or for 
breach of any terms and conditions of the licence by giving a notice of 15 days. 
4.22 Notwithstanding anyting contained anywhere else in the licence the 
Government's decision shall be final and conclusive. 
4.23 The licensees shall furnish a bank guarantee for a sum of Rs. 50,000/-(Rupees 
fifty thousand) only to ensure timely performance of the licence agreement. 
4.24 If the licensee fail to commission services within the stipulated period, he shall 
forfeit the amount of bank guarantee to the Government and the Government would 
be free to cancel the licence awarded to the licensee. 
4.25 A licence will be subject to such other conditions as may be determined 
by the Government.

Policy for education of special children 
4600. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any policy for the education of 'Special Children' 
i.e. children suffering from Cerebral Palsy, etc.; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the achievements of the last three years of National Trust for Welfare of 
Persons suffering from Cerebral Palsy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (DR. SANJAY PASWAN) : (a) and (b) The Policy framework for 
education of disabled children has been laid down in the "Persons with Disabilities 
Act, 1995" which inter-alia casts obligation on appropriate Governments to 
provide for the following: 
• Every child with disability shall have the right to free education till the age of 
18 years in regular or special schools. 
• Transportation, removal of architectural barriers and restructuring of 
curriculum and modifications in the examination system shall be ensured for the 
benefit of children with disabilities. 
172 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
• Children with disabilities shall be provided books, scholarships, uniform and 
other learning material. 
• Special schools for children with disabilities shall be equipped with 
vocational training facilities. 
• Government run educational institutes and other educational institutes 
receiving grant from Government shall reserve at least 3% seats for 
admission of persons with disabilities. 
Within the ambit of this framework the Ministry is implementing, a scheme through 
non-organizations, for setting up special schools and the Department of Secondary 
and Higher Education is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Integrated 
Education for Disabled Children. Children with cerebral palsy can therefore join 
regular or special programmes. 
(c) The National Trust for Welfare of persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, 
Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities, since its inception, has registered 334 
NGOs and set up 369 Local Level Committees to address guardianships issues. 
Under the Reach and Relief Scheme 103 projects directly benefiting 5000 
beneficiaries through Day Care Centres, Respite care centres, Permanent Care 
Centres and 100 Caregivers Training Programme benefiting 1400 home based 
caregivers have been sanctioned. Besides, Trust has taken initiatives in establishing 
information centres, organizing awareness campaign, seminars etc.

4617. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN : Will the Ministry of TRIBAL

consideration by the State Government, including the ordering of a magisterial 
inquiry into the matter. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has also requested the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, to take up the matter of a 
judicial inquiry with the State Government.

Implementation of the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992 
4627. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA : 
SHRI MOTJLAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state : 
(a) the status of implementation of the Constitution (74th Amendment) 
Act of 1992; 
(b) whether the implementation of the said Act is uniform in all the States 
and Union Territories; 
(c) if not, the steps taken by Government to ensure its implementation; 
(d) the States and Union Territories, which are yet to implement the Act; 
and 
(e) whether Government have drawn an action plan or target date by 
which the defaulter States can be forced to implement the Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHIR PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN) : (a) to (e) The Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 
1992 came into force on 1-6-1993. As provided in the Act, States/Union 
Territories were required to take action to bring the State Municipal Acts in 
conformity with the provisions of the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 
1992 within a period of one year from 1-6-1993. Following this, States/Union 
Territories amended their Municipal Acts to bring them in conformity with the 
provisions of the above Act. The amended Municipal Acts provide for 
constitution and composition of the Municipalities, fixed duration of 5 years, 
reservation of seats for SC, ST and women, setting up of State Finance 
Commission and State Election Commission, Setting up of District Planning 
Committees and Metropolitan Planning Committees. Following the amended 
provisions, States/Union Territories except Jharkhand and Pondicherry have 
conducted elections to Municipalities. State Finance Commissions have also 
been constituted to review the financial positions of the Municipalities in 
different States. The provisions relating to compositions, constitution and 
duration to Municipalities, reservation of seats for SC/ST and women, setting 
206 

RAJYA SABHA [5 May, 2003] 
up of State Finance Commission and State Election Commission and also setting 
up of District Planning Committees and Metropolitan Planning Committees 
are uniform to all States, as these are mandatory provisions prescribed in the 
Constitution (74th Amendment) Act.

4637. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND

(a) whether it is a fact that the Chief Vigilance Officer of DDA had stated in his

noticed at two institutional sites. The details of the report are as under:—

room service for food and other facilities were being provided in the hotel. A big

ground floor, space had been rented out to Industrial Development Bank of India 
(IDBI). 
(ii) Plot No. 1, East Patel Nagar, Institutional Area, New Delhi had been allotted 
to Bharonji Mandir Society but on the site a hotel having 35 rooms with facilities of 
AC, TV and attached toilets was running. Lift facility was also available, At the entrance 
of the hotel, in a very small space Bharonji Temple had been established.

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state:

Organisation (CGEWHO), an autonomous body under the administrative control of his

Phase-Ill, Sector-82;

giving individual connections to the dwelling units, directly by Uttar Pradesh Power 
Corporation instead of single point bulk supply, is expected soon. On obtaining the power

another big source of power. Experts say that if bunds are built in the 
catchment areas of Brahamaputra, it can generate about 70,000 MW, which is

only the demand of whole North-Eastern region, but the demands of some

made more efficient to transmit the produced electricity quickly to any part of

electricity bill given to individual consumers. On the other hand, pilferage of

some of the functionaries of authority connive, directly or indirectly, with the 
consumers. This happens, particularly, in industrial sector.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): The 
motions for consideration of the Appropriation (No.3) Bill, 2003 and the

DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I must say that our hon. Finance Minister has tried to be 
conscious, cautious and judicious in submitting the Budget by considering 
various aspects of the financial issues, but he has failed to accelerate the 
economy, I must say. The Indian economy, the GDP growth, the reduction of 
the fiscal deficit, and increase in the employment potentialities are very much 
interlinked with the industrial and agricultural growth. Due to unprecedented 
drought the growth of agriculture has very much been hampered. So far as 
industrial growth is concerned, there are several factors that are interlinked 
with it. The most important factor of them is the capital growth. I draw the 
attention of the hon. Finance Minister to the fact that despite a lot of efforts 
on the part of the NDA Government, the capital market is absolutely zero. 
They have inspired and made a lot of modifications in the SEBI. But, as on 
today, if any new industry has to be started in India, if any industry has to 
raise the capital from the public, it cannot; nobody can raise any money. This 
situation has not been there for one or two days, but for years together. The 
capital market is totally zero. So, I would like the Finance Minister to tell us 
in his reply as to what he is going to do, or, how he is going to solve the 
problem of reviving the capital market. 
The other most important point is this. I will just give one small 
example. If anybody wants to set up an industry in this country, what are the 
ways to get the finance needed? One is capital market, second is raising term 
loans from institutions, and the third is getting some foreign investments. In 
our country, the prime institutions like, the IFCI, IDBI, etc. have, virtually, 
become sick. Though they played a very important role for decades in 
providing finance to a number of industries, but, today, they are absolutely in 
a very bad shape. The industrial finance corporations, virtually, have got 
heavy losses, and they are not in a position to give any finance to any new 
industry. 
Similarly, IDBI also is not in a position to give any term loans to 
any industry. Then, the ICICI is there; the ICICI has been converted into 
ICICI Bank. The ICICI Bank, of course, is supposed to be a sound institution.    
It is a sound institution, but; recently, there was a big rumour 
275 

RAJYA SABHA              [5 May, 2003] 
that the ICICI Bank has also become sick. And people were standing in a 
queue to take back their deposits. However, it has been confirmed by the 
Government that it is not sick. My point is, this Bank cannot give major term 
loans to the industries. So, ICICI Bank, though we may consider it to be very 
sound, is not going to play a very big role in building up industries in our 
country. Now, if the IDBI also wants to revive itself, there are only two or 
three options left. One is: it must become an IDBI Bank, that is, it must merge 
with the IDBI Bank, or, the Government must give sufficient funding, which 
may not be possible. Therefore, it looks as if the Government is going to put it 
before the Standing Committee of Finance to consider converting it also into 
an IDBI Bank. Assuming that IDBI also becomes IDBI Bank, and 
Government permits it to raise the money from the public for self-reliance, 
then, what is going to happen to industries? Then, the IDBI Bank also cannot 
given loans to any new industry. So, IDBI has gone, ICICI cannot give loans; 
it is very sick, then, how do you expect industrial growth in this country? If 
there is no industrial growth, then, GDP is halted, deficit financing stops, 
employment stops, and the entire growth of the economy is stopped. So, this 
is a very important issue. So, with regard to capital market and financial 
institutions, I want the hon. "Finance Minister to clarify in this reply whether 
they are going to give some more funds to the IDBI. Even if IDBI becomes a 
bank, is the Government going to take a stand that they must give term loans 
for industries? And, also, in this connection, my submission is: If the IDBI 
Bank or the IDBI, whatever it may be, if they are allowed capital gains tax-
free bonds, or, even the tax-free bonds with low interest, perhaps, they will be 
able to raise some more money, and it will be of less burden to the 
Government. So, I request the hon. Finance Minister to bear in mind these 
things.

of the nation's economy is that there is agricultural and industrial failure.

very optimistic. It is good that he is planning to reduce the fiscal deficit. But,

year also he was very optimistic; he expected that

introduction of VAT, or, our Party is not against the VAT. I would like to

community, or, rather the entire community must be convinced. Nobody's 
feelings should be hurt. The interest of the entire trading system should not be 
affected. So, we must think more deeply, more carefully and more 
consciously, and see to it how best the trading community and also the entire 
business community grows smoothly. At the same time, we should get 
maximum revenue for the exchequer through the new-system, by simplifying 
the procedure of VAT. Sir, they say that the VAT is a simplified procedure. 
Had it been a simplified procedure, nobody would have been agitated over it. 
Therefore, I think, we must put in mo re efforts through va rious channels, in 
order to see that everybody is convinced and satisfied at the grass root level 
and at the bottom level, and only then, it should be introduced. 
Sir, the other thing is about our national exchequer. It is suffering 
for want of money. We want money. There is a fiscal deficit. In this 
connection, I would like to suggest one thing. The tax arrears are to the 
279 

RAJYA SABHA               [5 May. 2003] 
tune of Rs. 90,176 crores. There are matters pending in various courts and in 
the Appellate Tribunals in various parts of the country. Why should not the 
Government take a dynamic stand for one-time settlement of all these 
disputes, so that more money could be raised? If you see the statistics of the 
tax arrears, you will find that from last year to this year, it has gone up by Rs. 
30,000 crores. Next year, perhaps, this figure may rise to Rs. 1,20,000 crores. 
Why does the Finance Ministry not make an effort to minimise the litigations 
as far as possible? This issue was also raised by the Public Accounts 
Committee. For several years, we have been trying to suggest to the 
Government to adopt this line, but, till now, there is no result. So, I am calling 
upon the Finance Minister to bear it in mind and make an effort to raise more 
funds by settling disputes relating to these tax arrears, and strengthen the 
financial system of the country. 
Sir, I am happy that recently the Government has decided to buy 24 
per cent illiquid Government of India securities from the various commercial 
banks at the face value of Rs. 80,000 crores which is definitely a welcome 
measure. That has been'announced in the Budget also. If you do it, you will be 
able to reduce the interest burden of the Government, and also the burden of 
the various banks which will have better balance sheets by wiping out their 
liabilities and NPAs. Sir, I would like to make one suggestion regarding the 
MPLADS Fund. It was good that the Government had enhanced this amount 
to Rs. 2 crores. But, at the moment, each Member of Parliament has been 
requesting the Government to enhance this amount and make it Rs. 3 crores. 
Here, I would like to say very clearly-that there are various places in the 
constituency, where for want of a small bridge or a small road or a small 
under-tunnel, the entire communication is cut-off, and there are villages 
where,.there is no communication at all for ten days, for fifteen days, at a 
time, because of these shortcomings. In such cases, the Member of Parliament 
will immediately be able to spare Rs. 5 lakhs or Rs. 10 lakhs out of the 
MPLADS Fund for a small bridge or for a community hall for the poor people 
in his constituency. So, it is helpful in so many ways. In other words, it is the 
Member of Parliament, who is supposed to be in touch with the people, and 
who knows the difficulties of the people of his constituency and can take an 
on the spot decision to redress those difficulties. So, he should have the power 
and authority to allocate funds through the District Collector. Here, I would 
like to clarify one thing. There is a misunderstanding that these funds are 
being misused by the Members of Parliament. It is totally wrong. Why? 
Because, there is no chance for any Member of Parliament to misuse these 
funds. The funds are 
280 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
used through the District Collector. The District Collector has to follow 
certain rules while allocating such funds. He has to call the tenders, has to 
make the estimates and has to cross-check the entire thing, and whatever 
allotment is made, should also be within the purview of the rules. Therefore, 
there is no chance for its being misused, and whatever money is spent, is 
being spent for the development of our own villages. Sir, for the purpose of 
rural development, we are giving thousands of crores of .rupees. They are 
also meant for the development of villages and other basic infrastructure in 
the rural areas. But, the unfortunate thing is that for want of proper 
communication, there is no proper utilisation of these funds. There is no 
coordination; there is no system in the Rural Development Ministry to ensure 
proper funding. Rs. 50.000 crores to Rs. 60,000 crores are given by this 
Ministry to various States. When we make a request to this Ministry to allot 
more funds, they say: "It is not in our hands. We depend on the States." Some 
times, if the States are not able to spend the amount which has been allocated 
to them, in that case, the Rural Development Ministry will not release the 
money. When the States have been allocated certain funds by the Government 
of India, and when the States have not fully utilised those funds, who is 
responsible for not spending these funds fully? It is the States who are 
responsible. Who are the sufferers on this count? It is the people who are the 
sufferers on this count. Who is responsible for this problem? It is the system 
itself. This problem aiso arises due to lack of communication'. So, if the 
States do not spend the money allocated to them by the Central Government, 
the Central Government must question them why they have failed on this 
count and why they have not been able to spend those funds meant for the 
villages and the poor people. Therefore, till the time a proper system is 
developed, and till the time proper utilisation of these funds take place, it will 
be more viable and more useful that the MPs are given authority to allocate 
funds in their constituencies because, they have got the first hand information 
about the problems of their constituencies. This is very much desirable. 
Almost 95 per cent of the MPs, if not 100 per cent, are asking for this 
increase in the MPLAD fund. There may be some, who may oppose this 
suggestion. But, the hon. Finance Minister  is saying that there is no money. I 
would suggest that you can adjust this increase in the allocation of the Rural 
Development Ministry, because there are umpteen number of cases where the 
full amount allocated for a particular scheme has not been spent on that 
scheme. There are so many schemes. People have no idea or knowledge about 
these schemes. Therefore, I am requesting the hon. Finance Minister to 
enhance this amount.

RAJYA SABHA              [5 May, 2003] 
Then, another point is, there is a 20-point economic programme. The 
Government has come forward with a scheme to help the poor people by way 
of self-employment. They have also announced certain self-employment 
schemes for women by allowing the facility of loans through the nationalised 
banks for community development. My question is, it is not taking place. 
There are a number of commercial banks and nationalised banks, who are not 
sticking to these programmes. So, I request the Finance Minister to bear in 
mind this thing and question the management of various banks to ensure 
whether they are really followings the guidelines in this regard, and whether 
they are giving loans accordingly or not. The major problem is the problem of 
unemployment. Of course, we criticize the Government for not creating one 
crore jobs, as it had promised; it has failed. But besides this criticism, I have 
to make a constructive suggestion also. Besides Government raising 
employment opportunities, they must create self-employment schemes also. 
The graduates are there; today, a graduate is frustrated. He chooses the wrong 
path because there is no job for him anywhere. If the banks extend some help 
in generating self-employment, he will definitely take it up. Here, my 
submission is, there is nobody to guide them. There are banks, which must 
provide some help, as per the norms set by the Government and the Reserve 
Bank of India. But people do not know how to use the facilities that are 
available in the banks. So, I would request the hon. Finance Minister to see to 
it that a system is built, where you can communicate with the concerned 
people in the villages, and places where the graduates, poor women, peasants 
and people from all walks of life, who are eligible to avail the facilities of the 
Government through the banks, and help them to take up self-employment or 
small business. Thus, they can lead a happy life. But this is not taking place. 
Hence, you must sef up machinery through which you are able to extend this 
great help to the community. I shall finish my speech in ten minutes. 
Another very important point is, today, in the country, virtually 90 
per cent of the State Governments are in a financial crisis. They have no 
money to pay salaries to employees. Even if the World Bank, ADB or other 
international organisations provide loan to them, they have to first spend 
money, which then has to be reimbursed. But they have no money to invest. 
Thirdly, there is a financial crisis. We are not able to take up many projects 
and welfare activities for want of money. This has not been going on since a 
day, but for the past 10 "years or so. In 1990, the gross fiscal deficit was Rs. 
18,000 crores in the country. Now, the deficit is Rs. one lakh two thousand 
crores. Imagine, in ten years, it has jumped from Rs. 18,000 
282 

[5 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
crores to Rs. one lakh two thousand crores. This is the gross deficit finance in 
the State Governments. I do not wish to name the States. But this is how the 
State Governments are suffering. In a number of States, about 95 per cent of 
the States, there is a financial crisis. So, my question to the hon. Finance 
Minister is, what is the solution? After all, State finance and Central finance is 
inter-linked. If the State is so poor, you cannot expect the Centre to be rich. 
Therefore, my submission is that this is a very serious matter. I am rather 
surprised that for the last four to five years, the Government has not come 
forward to salvage such a serious situation. For example, you may see, the 
State Governments not only borrowed a net amount of Rs. thirteen thousand 
six hundred and twenty two crores in 2002-03, but also resorted to a 
supplementary amount of Rs. fifteen thousand four hundred and twenty two 
crores. Of the last mentioned, Rs. ten thousand crores was for a debt swap 
scheme, to retire the high-cost deficits. And also, if you see the fiscal position 
of the States, have been witnessing a continuous deterioration during the 
period 1996-97 to 1999-2000. It has shown some improvement in 2001; but it 
is a very small improvement. Before 1999, it was about Rs. 91,000 crores; in 
one year, it was less by to Rs. 2000. Then again, it jumped up. According to 
the revised estimates for 2001-02, the States' GFD, that is, the gross fiscal 
deficit, goes to Rs. one lakh six thousand five hundred and ninety five crores, 
that is, 4.9 per cent of GDP, which was higher than the Budget scheme. 
(Time-bell) Now, I shall make sum up the overall situation in a nutshell. As I 
said, the hon. Finance Minister has tried to be conscious, cautious and 
judicious, but has failed to accelerate the economy. We do have an accelerator 
in our hands, but are not able to accelerate the economy. This is because 
industrial growth and agricultural production have failed to accelerate, with 
unprecedented drought on the one hand and various other factors on the other. 
Today, there is so much of fiscal deficit, the GDP growth has fallen down and 
the States are in a financial crisis. The sugar industry is jn a serious and 
unprecedented crisis. For the last 50 years, it has never happened. The rate 
has fallen down from Rs. 15/- to Rs. 10.50. It is a phenomenal crisis. Nobody 
would appreciate this step. Unless the Government comes forward to solve 
the crisis with determination, dedication, devotion and concentration, things 
won't improve. He has to convince us as to how he is going to improve the 
fiscal deficit position. There is a shorta ge of Rs. 1 crore ahd 36 lakhs. How is 
he going to raise the amount of revenue? Last year, he had failed to collect so 
much revere. This year, he may be overoptimistic. How is he going to fill up 
the gap? Last year also, we had suffered due to a severe drought.   As the 
283 

RAJYA SABHA                [5 May. 2003] 
pundits have anticipated, this year also, there is going to be a drought. What 
measures does he contemplate to take to revamp the financial structure and 
system if the drought continues this year also? Our hon. Finance Minister has 
presented the Budget in a very, very serious crisis because the entire financial 
system is in a very difficult state; there is no new industry; no new 
production; the industries are mostly sick, and there is no chance for 
economic growth. Despite all this, he has not increased the tax rates; and has 
given, of course, a lot of fiscal incentives. Still I feel that, though certain 
things are not possible, if he makes much more concerted efforts, accept it as 
a challenge, and take it to a point that India should be glorious, he must be 
able to compete with China with complete determination, he can achieve the 
goals. Every citizen will also take it as a challenge, provided the Government 
comes forward, bearing in mind all the difficulties the country is facing. In 
conclusion, let us not forget that the small-scale industries, cottage industries, 
medium industries and the agricultural production are the livewires of India's 
growth. He must concentrate more and more on them. Merely saying 'okay, 
we have made efforts for capital growth, we have strengthened the financial 
institution' won't help. Institutions are there. Sir, I want a categorical 
statement, a clear-cut clarification as to how he is going to do it with IDBI 
alone. I am stressing the word 'IDBI' because it is the only institution in the 
country, which gives money for industrial growth. There is no other 
institution. ICICI has become a bank. It is dominated by private people. There 
is only one institution, IDBI. How is he going to improve the Indian economy, 
the economic growth rate and the GDP growth rate?

whole year, without restricting it to the khariff crop only. In certain States, 
both the crops were affected due to the unprecedented drought. 
The scheme of interest relief to be met by the Government of India 
should cover the entire year, 2002-03. The NABARD has restricted the 
conversion of short-term loans into medium-term loans for unirrigated crops 
for khariff crop, 2002. 
I urge upon the Government that the conversion of short-term loans 
to the medium term-loans should be extended to irrigated land also to 
mitigate the hardships of farmers affected by drought. This should also cover 
the rabi season, which is the main season in Tamil Nadu. 
The crucial issue is the pricing of diesel and petroleum products. 
Due to dismantling- of the Administered Price Mechanism, the prices of 
petro-products are fluctuating as per the world market price of crude oil. 
There must be a transparent system to index the prevailing world market 
price with the retail rates of diesel and petrol. 
Sir, after the Petroleum Ministry has put an end to the cross 
subsidization of petroleum products, the Government linked the petrol and 
diesel prices in the domestic market to the prices prevailing in the 
international market. But, the Ministry has been in the practice of raising the 
prices whenever crude prices went up in the international market. But the 
Government kept mum when the prices in the international market came 
down. For, example, the petrol prices were hiked by nearly Rs. 5 per litre 
citing Iraq War. But, after the US Fo rces captured Iraq, and the international 
prices of crude fell rapidly by about 12 dollars per barrel, the Government of 
India mislead the consumers and brought down the prices by only one rupee 
per litre. This practice on the customers should be stopped, or, the 
Government should scrap tne scheme of linking domestic prices with the 
international market. Moreover, the Government is also periodically hiking 
the prices of diesel, Now, the diesel prices are almost on par with the petrol 
prices. The diesel prices hike means hike in the prices of all essential 
commodities, and the inflation will raise its head once again. Since the price 
of crude has fallen rapidly, the Government should reduce the prices of both 
petrol and diesel.

make my observations regarding the Finance Bill as well as the Appropriation

tremendous amount of homework he has done. Through this Finance Bill,

compensation, to the tune of five lakh rupees. Also exemption has been 
allowed to the income accrued by the ex-servicemen corporations. The 
writers can deduct a royalty up to Rs. three lakhs from the income. The 
royalty income for the services of the s ecurity of Indian Services is totally 
removed from this. 
'[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair.]

one. The expenditure tax on the chargeable expenditure in hotels, i.e. about 
Rs.3,000, rent and other things, is also welcome. The long-term capital gains, 
if invested in equity, would not attract income tax. It is a welcome step.
